path: Restriction, quantification, and satisfying paths for BDDs

uses: Reduced ordered binary decision diagrams: canonicity and apply

results.title: Restriction of a binary decision diagram
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a variable $x$ and a Boolean $b$, the restriction (cofactor) $t[x := b]$ of a binary decision diagram $t$ is defined recursively: a leaf is kept; a node testing $x$ is replaced by the restriction of its $\mathrm{hi}$ child if $b$ is true and of its $\mathrm{lo}$ child if $b$ is false; and a node testing any other variable $v$ is rebuilt from the restrictions of its two children with the reducing node…

results.title: Restriction yields a reduced diagram
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every binary decision diagram $t$, every variable $x$ and every Boolean $b$, the cofactor $t[x := b]$ is reduced: no node has two equal children.

results.title: Restriction yields an ROBDD
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $t$ is an ordered binary decision diagram (tested variables strictly increase along every path), then for every variable $x$ and every Boolean $b$ the cofactor $t[x := b]$ is a reduced ordered binary decision diagram.

results.title: Existential quantification of a diagram
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a variable $x$ and a binary decision diagram $t$, the existential quantification of $t$ over $x$ is the diagram obtained by combining the cofactors $t[x := \mathrm{false}]$ and $t[x := \mathrm{true}]$ with Bryant's apply under disjunction.

results.title: Universal quantification of a diagram
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a variable $x$ and a binary decision diagram $t$, the universal quantification of $t$ over $x$ is the diagram obtained by combining the cofactors $t[x := \mathrm{false}]$ and $t[x := \mathrm{true}]$ with Bryant's apply under conjunction.

results.title: Existential quantification yields an ROBDD
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $t$ is an ordered binary decision diagram (tested variables strictly increase along every path), then for every variable $x$ the existential quantification of $t$ over $x$ is a reduced ordered binary decision diagram.

results.title: Satisfying path of a binary decision diagram
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The satisfying path of a diagram is found by a depth-first search for a leaf $\mathrm{true}$ that tries the $\mathrm{hi}$ (true) child of each node before its $\mathrm{lo}$ (false) child. It is returned as the list of pairs $(v, c)$ of the variables $v$ tested along the path with the branches $c$ taken (empty at a leaf $\mathrm{true}$), and the search returns nothing when the diagram has no leaf $\mathrm{true}$.

results.title: Assignment read off a path
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a path $p$, given as a list of pairs $(v, b)$ of a variable $v \in \mathbb{N}$ and a Boolean $b$, the assignment read off $p$ sends a variable $x$ to the Boolean of the first pair in $p$ whose variable is $x$, and to $\mathrm{false}$ if $x$ occurs in no pair of $p$.

results.title: The path assignment satisfies an ordered diagram
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary decision diagram ordered from some $n$ (every tested variable is at least $n$, and tested variables strictly increase along every path). If the satisfying-path search on $t$ returns a path $p$, then $t$ evaluates to true under the assignment read off $p$.

results.title: Reduced diagrams other than false have a satisfying path
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a binary decision diagram $t$ is reduced and is not the leaf $\mathrm{false}$, then the search for a satisfying path in $t$ succeeds: it returns a path from the root of $t$ to a leaf $\mathrm{true}$.

results.title: Satisfiability with one variable fixed to false
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a proposition over atoms indexed by natural numbers, let $t$ be its ROBDD, and let $f$ be a natural number. Then $A$ evaluates to true under some valuation $\sigma$ with $\sigma(f) = \mathrm{false}$ if and only if the cofactor $t[f := \mathrm{false}]$ is not the leaf $\mathrm{false}$.

results.title: Satisfy-one with a variable fixed to false
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a proposition over natural-number atoms and let $f$ be a natural number. If some assignment $\sigma$ with $\sigma(f) = \mathrm{false}$ satisfies $A$, then the search for a satisfying path in the restriction at $f := \mathrm{false}$ of the ROBDD of $A$ returns a path $p$, and the assignment read off $p$ (the recorded value on each variable of $p$, false elsewhere), changed to send $f$ to $\mathrm{false}$,…

results.title: The all-true valuation satisfies every proposition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every proposition $A$ over atoms indexed by natural numbers, built from atoms with $\land$, $\lor$ and $\to$ only, evaluates to true under the valuation that makes every atom true.

results.title: Satisfy-one for propositions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every proposition $A$ over atoms indexed by natural numbers, the satisfying-path search on the ROBDD of $A$ returns a path $p$, and $A$ evaluates to true under the assignment read off $p$.

results.title: Clauses containing a variable only positively
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a variable $x$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$, the formula consisting of the clauses of $\varphi$, in their order, that contain the literal $x$ and do not contain the literal $\neg x$.

results.title: Clauses containing a variable only negatively
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a variable $x$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$, the formula consisting of the clauses of $\varphi$, in their order, that contain the literal $\neg x$ and do not contain the literal $x$.

results.title: Davis-Putnam elimination of a variable
results.caption: Definition
results.summary:
Eliminating a variable $x$ from a CNF formula $\varphi$ gives the formula consisting of the clauses of $\varphi$ that contain neither $x$ nor $
eg x$, followed by the resolvents on $x$ of $C$ and $D$, for every clause $C$ of $\varphi$ that contains $x$ but not $
eg x$ and every clause $D$ of $\varphi$ that contains $
eg x$ but not $x$. Clauses containing both $x$ and $
eg x$ are dropped.

results.title: Resolvents do not mention the resolved variable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a variable and let $C$ and $D$ be clauses such that $C$ does not contain $\neg x$ and $D$ does not contain $x$. Then no literal of the resolvent of $C$ and $D$ on $x$ has variable $x$.

results.title: Soundness of a Davis-Putnam step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a variable and $\varphi$ a CNF formula. Every assignment that satisfies $\varphi$ also satisfies the formula obtained from $\varphi$ by eliminating $x$.

results.title: Completeness of a Davis-Putnam step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a variable, $\varphi$ a CNF formula and $\sigma$ an assignment that satisfies the formula obtained from $\varphi$ by eliminating $x$. Then there is a truth value $b$ such that the assignment that agrees with $\sigma$ except that it sends $x$ to $b$ satisfies $\varphi$.

results.title: Davis-Putnam elimination preserves satisfiability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every variable $x$ and every CNF formula $\varphi$, the formula obtained from $\varphi$ by eliminating $x$ is satisfiable if and only if $\varphi$ is satisfiable.

results.title: Successive elimination of a list of variables
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ of variables and a CNF formula $\varphi$, eliminate $x_1$ from $\varphi$, then $x_2$ from the result, and so on up to $x_n$. For the empty list the result is $\varphi$.

results.title: Variable list for Davis–Putnam elimination
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a CNF formula $\varphi$, the list of the variables occurring in the literals of $\varphi$, each listed exactly once, in order of first occurrence when the clauses of $\varphi$, and the literals within each clause, are read from left to right.

results.title: The Davis-Putnam procedure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a CNF formula $\varphi$, eliminate the variables that occur in $\varphi$ one after another, each exactly once, in the order of their first occurrence in $\varphi$, each elimination being applied to the result of the previous one. The procedure returns true if the resulting formula does not contain the empty clause, and false if it does.

results.title: Correctness of the Davis-Putnam procedure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every CNF formula $\varphi$, the Davis-Putnam procedure returns true on $\varphi$ if and only if $\varphi$ is satisfiable.

results.title: Groups with exactly one irreducible representation of each dimension
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ has exactly one irreducible complex representation of each dimension when for every $n \ge 1$ there is an irreducible homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ and any two irreducible homomorphisms $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ are equivalent. Representations are arbitrary homomorphisms of the abstract group $G$; no continuity is required.

results.title: McKay's question on $\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$ (Kourovka 16.58)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ has exactly one irreducible complex representation of each dimension $n = 1, 2, \dots$, up to equivalence, if and only if $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$. Here a representation of dimension $n$ is any homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ of abstract groups, with no continuity required.

results.title: McKay's question 16.58 has a negative answer

results.summary: It is not the case that a group has exactly one irreducible complex representation of each dimension $n \ge 1$, up to equivalence, if and only if it is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$. Here a representation of dimension $n$ is any homomorphism to $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ of abstract groups, with no continuity required.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The closed testing procedure: given the decisions `φ J` of local tests of the intersection hypotheses `H_J`, reject `Hᵢ` exactly when `φ J` holds for every `J` containing `i`.

results.title: Closed testing rejection implies the intersection test rejects
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the closed procedure rejects a hypothesis in `H0`, then the local test of the intersection hypothesis `H_{H0}` rejects.

results.title: The closed testing principle
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `H0` is the set of true nulls and the local test of `H_{H0}` rejects with probability at most `α`, then the closed procedure rejects some true null with probability at most `α`. Applied to every possible `H0`, local level-`α` tests give strong control of the family-wise error rate. No assumption on the dependence between local tests is made.

results.title: Level of the Bonferroni local test

results.title: Holm's procedure is a closed test

results.title: Induced forest number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, the induced forest number $a(G)$ is the maximum number of vertices of an induced forest in $G$, that is, the maximum cardinality of a set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced on $S$ is acyclic.

results.title: Induced forests are no larger than the induced forest number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$. For every set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced on $S$ is acyclic, $|S|$ is at most the induced forest number of $G$.

results.title: The induced forest number is at most the number of vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, the induced forest number of $G$ is at most $|V|$.

results.title: The induced forest number is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, there is a set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced on $S$ is acyclic and $|S|$ equals the induced forest number of $G$.

part.title: Moore's algorithm
api: Moore class of a reachable state

uses: Decision procedures for automata, grammars and strings
Least and greatest fixed points on finite sets

results.title: Moore refinement step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with state set $S$ and transition function $\delta$. One round of Moore's refinement sends a set $E \subseteq S \times S$ of pairs of states to the set of pairs $(p, q) \in S \times S$ such that $p$ is accepting if and only if $q$ is accepting and, for every letter $a$, the pair $(\delta(p, a), \delta(q, a))$ lies in $E$.

results.title: Stopping Moore iteration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, and write $R$ for one round of Moore's refinement. For a set $E$ of pairs of states of $M$ and a budget $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the stopping Moore iteration is defined by recursion on $n$: with budget $0$ it returns $E$; with budget $n + 1$ it returns $E$ if $R(E) = E$, and otherwise the stopping Moore iteration from $R(E)$ with budget $n$.

results.title: Output of the stopping Moore iteration
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, and write $R$ for one round of Moore's refinement. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every set $E$ of pairs of states of $M$, there is $k \le n$ such that the stopping Moore iteration from $E$ with budget $n$ returns $R^k(E)$, and if $k < n$ then $R^k(E)$ is a fixed point of $R$, that is, $R(R^k(E)) = R^k(E)$.

results.title: Moore's relation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finite set of states $Q$, Moore's relation is the set of pairs of states obtained from $Q \times Q$ by repeating rounds of Moore's refinement until a round changes nothing, for at most $|Q \times Q|$ rounds.

results.title: Moore's relation contains every post-fixed point
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. If a set $Z$ of pairs of states of $M$ is contained in its image under one round of Moore's refinement, then $Z$ is contained in Moore's relation of $M$.

results.title: Correctness of Moore's refinement
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, two states $p$ and $q$ of $M$ are related by Moore's relation if and only if they have the same continuation language: for every word $w$, $M$ started at $p$ accepts $w$ exactly when $M$ started at $q$ accepts $w$.

results.title: Moore equivalence on reachable states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$, two reachable states $p$ and $q$ of $M$ are related when the pair $(p, q)$ lies in Moore's relation of $M$; this relation is an equivalence relation on the reachable states of $M$.

results.title: States of Moore's automaton
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$, these are the equivalence classes of the reachable states of $M$ under Moore equivalence, that is, under Moore's relation of $M$ restricted to reachable states. They are the states of Moore's minimal automaton.

results.title: Moore class of a reachable state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. For a reachable state $s$ of $M$, its Moore class is the equivalence class of $s$ among the reachable states of $M$ under Moore's relation; it is a state of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$.

results.title: Moore's minimal automaton
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ has as states the classes of reachable states of $M$ under Moore's relation. Its start state is the class of the start state of $M$; reading a letter $a$ sends the class of a reachable state $s$ to the class of the state that $M$ reaches from $s$ on $a$; and the class of $s$ is accepting exactly when $s$ is an accepting…

results.title: Moore's automaton accepts the same language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ accepts exactly the language accepted by $M$.

results.title: Continuation language of a Moore class
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. Each state of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$, a class of reachable states of $M$, is sent to the continuation language of any member $s$, the set of words that $M$ accepts when started at $s$; this is a reachable residual language of $M$. It does not depend on the choice of $s$, because Moore-related states have the same continuation language.

results.title: Moore classes are the reachable residuals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. The states of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ are in bijection with the reachable residual languages of $M$: the bijection sends the class of a reachable state $s$ to the continuation language of $s$, the set of words that $M$ accepts when started at $s$.

results.title: Moore's automaton is the minimal automaton
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. Renaming each state of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$, a class of reachable states, to the continuation language accepted from its members turns Moore's automaton into exactly the minimized DFA of $M$, whose states are the reachable continuation languages of $M$.

results.title: Moore's automaton has one state per Nerode class
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ has exactly as many states as there are Nerode classes of the language accepted by $M$.

results.title: Generating function of the Poisson distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Poisson(`r`) generating function: `∑ e^{-r} r^k / k! x^k = exp (r (x - 1))`.

results.title: Mean of the Poisson distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Poisson(`r`) law has mean `r`.

results.title: Haldane's survival probability of a mutant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Haldane's survival probability `π(s) = 1 - q(s)` of a mutant with selective advantage `s` per generation, whose number of copies in the next generation is Poisson with mean `1 + s`. The model needs `s ≥ -1`; for `s < -1` the mean is truncated to `0` (`Real.toNNReal`), the mutant leaves no copies, and `π(s) = 0`.

results.title: Haldane's equation for the survival probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `π(s)` solves Haldane's equation `1 - π = exp (-(1 + s) π)`.

results.title: Beneficial mutant survives with positive probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A beneficial mutant survives with positive probability.

results.title: Survival probability is less than one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The survival probability is less than `1`: the mutant leaves no copies with positive probability `exp (-(1 + s))`. (For `s < -1`, outside the model, `π(s) = 0`.)

results.title: Nonnegativity of the survival probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The survival probability is non-negative.

results.title: Haldane's approximation $\pi(s) \approx 2s$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Haldane's approximation (Haldane 1927): `π(s) / s → 2` as `s → 0⁺`.
